name: embraos-git
description: Self-hosted git servers: private-CA trust, per-host tokens, and the gl_* GitLab tools

nodes._comment: ── trust: how a private CA becomes trusted ──────────────

nodes.content: A private root CA becomes trusted from two places, both read at boot: certificate files (*.pem / *.crt) the image was built with, under /usr/share/embra/ca-certificates/ (the builder's Imported_CAs/ folder; read-only, and gone again with an image built without them), and the operator's drop-ins in /embra/state/ca-certificates/. embrad merges both with the stock public CA bundle and exports the result to every service via GIT_SSL_CAINFO and SSL_CERT_FILE — so git_clone, git_push, and git_pull trust self-hosted git servers behind a private CA (for example an mkcert development CA) while github.com and other public hosts keep working — and the brain's own HTTP clients add the same files as trust anchors. A certificate file takes effect at the NEXT BOOT, and nothing in a running system adds one: it is seeded while the machine is stopped, or built into the image.

A git tool failing with 'SSL certificate problem: unable to get local issuer certificate' against a self-hosted server means that server's CA is not in the trust bundle of this boot. What the boot had can be read: file_read lists /embra/state/ca-certificates/ and /usr/share/embra/ca-certificates/, and the brain's log counts what it loaded ('operator CA drop-ins: N certificate(s)', 'image CA certificates: N certificate(s)', a line for each directory that held any; system_logs with the filter 'certificate(s) from'). embrad's own line, 'Operator CA trust: merged …', names each accepted file, but it is printed before embrad's log file exists: it is on the serial line and the display at boot, and system_logs does not show it. The fix is the operator's, and which one depends on the machine: on a raw disk image, scripts/seed-state.sh --ca-dir with the machine stopped; on a machine installed from the ISO or run from a converted disk, an image built with the certificate in Imported_CAs/. A reboot follows either way.

embraOS has two TLS trust paths, and both honor the CA certificates of the operator and of the image. The git binary and other OpenSSL child processes read the boot-merged CA bundle (GIT_SSL_CAINFO / SSL_CERT_FILE). The brain's own HTTP clients carry compiled-in public roots and add the same certificate files as trust anchors: the LLM providers (which matters when they go through an HTTPS gateway with a CA of its own), the gl_* GitLab and gh_* GitHub tools, and the Guardian transport behind http_get and http_request. One client keeps the public roots alone: web_search's, which talks to Brave's API. A private-CA URL that works in git_clone therefore verifies in a Guardian http_request too (a private address additionally has to be on the operator's egress allowlist); when one path fails and the other does not, the cause is not the CA.

/git-token <host> <token> stores a per-host personal access token for self-hosted git servers. git_clone, git_push, and git_pull then authenticate to that host automatically (the token is injected as an oauth2 URL rewrite — clone URLs stay clean of credentials). /git-token with no arguments lists configured hosts without revealing token values; /git-token <host> remove deletes one. github.com is handled separately by /github-token — the two are not interchangeable.

The gl_* tools — gl_issues, gl_mrs, gl_issue_create, gl_mr_create — talk to a self-hosted GitLab instance's REST API. Each takes the GitLab hostname plus the FULL project path (group/repo, not just the repo name). Authentication is the /git-token personal access token for that host, which needs GitLab's 'api' scope. Their HTTP client trusts the operator CA drop-ins, so a private-CA instance verifies. Merge requests are GitLab's pull requests: gl_mrs lists them as !iid with source → target branches, and gl_mr_create opens one from an already-pushed branch.

The gh_* tools are GitHub-only — they call api.github.com and can never reach a self-hosted GitLab, whose API is incompatible (different endpoints, auth, and a merge-request rather than pull-request model). For a GitLab server, use the ordinary git tools for repository work (git_clone/git_push/git_pull work against any trusted host) and the gl_* set for issues and merge requests.

embraOS resolves names through the resolvers its DHCP lease names; under QEMU's user network that is the SLIRP gateway, which forwards to the host's real DNS. Entries in another machine's /etc/hosts are invisible inside embraOS. A self-hosted server's hostname must resolve from inside the OS; otherwise the operator needs an IP-address URL, which only verifies if the server certificate carries an IP subject-alternative-name.

nodes.title: Work with a self-hosted GitLab repository
nodes.description: End-to-end flow from trust to merge request against a self-hosted GitLab instance.
steps: Confirm the server's CA is trusted: its certificate must have been in /embra/state/ca-certificates/ or in the image's /usr/share/embra/ca-certificates/ at the last boot — file_read lists both directories, and system_logs (filter 'certificate(s) from') shows how many the brain loaded.
Confirm auth: /git-token should list the host; if not, ask the operator for a personal access token with the 'api' scope and store it with /git-token <host> <token>.
Branch, edit, commit, and git_push with the normal git tools — the stored token authenticates automatically.
Open the merge request with gl_mr_create (host, group/repo project path, title, source_branch, target_branch); track it later with gl_mrs.

outcomes.success: The clone, push, and merge-request cycle completes against the self-hosted instance with no credentials in URLs.
outcomes.failure: A TLS, auth, or DNS error — separate the cause with the 'Diagnose a failing self-hosted git connection' procedure instead of retrying blindly.

nodes.title: Diagnose a failing self-hosted git connection
nodes.description: Separate TLS, auth, and DNS causes before involving the operator — each has a distinct signature and a different fix.
steps: Read the exact error: 'unable to get local issuer certificate' is TLS trust; HTTP 401/403 is the token; 'Could not resolve host' is DNS.

TLS: file_read lists /embra/state/ca-certificates/ and /usr/share/embra/ca-certificates/, and system_logs (filter 'certificate(s) from') shows what the brain loaded at this boot — a server whose CA file is in neither directory is not trusted. Putting it there is an operator action (seed-state.sh --ca-dir on a raw disk image with the machine stopped, or an image built with the file in Imported_CAs/), and a reboot follows.
Auth: /git-token to list configured hosts; if the host is missing or the token expired, ask the operator to re-store it (gl_* tools additionally need the 'api' scope).
DNS: the hostname must resolve inside the OS — another machine's /etc/hosts does not apply; an IP URL works only when the certificate has an IP subject-alternative-name.
Report the identified cause to the operator — a CA cannot be added from inside a session, and a reboot is the operator's /reboot now.

outcomes.success: The failing layer is identified and either fixed in-session (token) or reported precisely (CA seed, reboot, DNS).
outcomes.failure: The error does not match any signature — capture the full tool error and the embrad log tail for the operator.

nodes._comment: ── the gl_* tool surface (2026-09-08 parity set) ────────

nodes.content: The gl_* GitLab tools cover a full work loop, not just listing: gl_issues / gl_mrs to list, gl_issue_view / gl_mr_view to read one item with its comment thread, gl_issue_create / gl_mr_create to open, gl_issue_comment / gl_mr_comment to discuss, gl_issue_close / gl_issue_reopen / gl_mr_close to change state, gl_mr_merge to merge, and gl_boards / gl_board_view for issue boards. The host argument is optional when exactly one host is configured through /git-token; two or more configured hosts is an error naming them, and github.com is never chosen implicitly.

GitLab's vocabulary differs from GitHub's in ways that change tool arguments. A merge request is GitLab's pull request and is addressed by its per-project iid (the !N in the UI), not a global id. Merging takes a squash boolean and a separate when_pipeline_succeeds flag rather than GitHub's merge_method. 'Project' means the repository itself, so GitHub Projects correspond to issue boards — which is why the tools are named gl_boards and gl_board_view.
